# Concluding Remarks: What This Element Does, and What Comes Next

## Revisiting Conceptual, Theoretical, and Analytical Approaches to Policy Learning

In the first chapter of this Element, we started with the question of why, how, and when policy actors do what they do, a question that has long been central to public policy scholarship. Among the different theoretical approaches developed to answer this question, policy learning stands out as one of the most pervasive and powerful, providing a coherent and robust account of why policy actors do what they do, as a function of how, why, and when they learn about policy problems [see @kamkhajiPolicyLearningEuro2022]. This view is premised on an overarching understanding of learning as policy-embedded, where policy actors seek and process information and knowledge about policy problems while embedded within a particular policy context, and where that information and knowledge interacts with the institutional structures around them [@zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. Policy-embedded learning is, in turn, a driver of policy behavior regardless of normative assessments of the quality of a given learning outcome, traceable to updates in policy-issue understandings and beliefs and, potentially from there, to updates in policy-related behaviors, from advocacy to varying degrees of policy change. By adopting this microfoundational perspective, policy learning is seen as central to individual and collective behavior.

Yet, as Chapter 1 argued, much of this rich literature foregrounds what changes in learning while leaving less explicit how such change is generated at the microfoundational level. Chapter 5 returned to this literature directly, revisiting the field's conceptual, analytical, and theoretical approaches to policy learning, summarized in @tbl-learn-concept, @tbl-learn-levels, and @tbl-learn-descript, and showing how the model and framework developed in this Element speak to each by giving process- and outcome-oriented definitions of learning a shared mechanism, giving the field's persistent aggregation problem across micro, meso, and macro levels a workable approach, and giving existing descriptor families a common underlying logic. We do not repeat that discussion here; instead, we briefly recap how the model and framework were developed before turning to their limitations and to avenues for future research.

## A Deeper Understanding of Policy Learning Dynamics: An Information Processing Approach

In Chapter 2, we examined the micro-foundations of how learning occurs, by tracing and analyzing the role of information, the building block or raw material of the learning process, and how it interacts with pre-existing beliefs and belief systems. To do so, we constructed a model of policy learning through information processing. This model focuses on belief change as the main learning outcome, operationalizing four varieties as a function of the interaction between pre-existing beliefs and information, including no learning, belief decay, belief reinforcement, and belief change. In Chapter 3, we then used many years' worth of public opinion data from the US about nuclear energy to explore this process, tracing how beliefs and preferences updated following the information signal about the risks of nuclear energy provided by the 2011 accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant in Japan. That example showed belief change regarding the risks and benefits of nuclear energy, as well as preference change regarding the construction of new nuclear power plants, congruent with the Fukushima information signal.

After developing the policy learning and information processing model in Chapters 2 and 3, in Chapter 4 we placed the micro-foundational model within the broader context of policymaking, which includes information, information processing by policy actors and institutions, and policy learning embedded within policy subsystems and governance structures. We also discussed pathways from policy learning to policy change, which includes belief change, preference change, behavior change, and policy change, and illustrated these pathways with brief vignettes of how several countries responded to the Fukushima accident. For policy change to happen as a result of policy learning through information processing, all elements must be aligned and consistent with the information. This means that belief change must be consistent with the information, preference change must be consistent with belief change, behavior change must be consistent with belief and preference change, and policy change must be consistent with belief, preference, and behavior change.

Finally, in Chapter 5 we returned to the broader policy learning literature to situate the our model and framework within it. We discussed how the model gives process-oriented, paradigmatic, and outcome-oriented conceptualizations of learning a shared underlying mechanism, rather than treating them as a family of loosely related definitions. We also noted that the framework offers an approach to the field's persistent problem of aggregating learning across micro, meso, and macro levels of analysis, illustrated through the multi-level Fukushima vignettes in Chapter 4. Finally, we showed how the model and framework speak to the field's most common descriptor families, namely forms, modes, mechanisms, types, and outcomes of learning, giving orders of change, modes of learning, and the loop-learning tradition a common underlying logic.

## What Comes Next? Avenues for Future Research

Having discussed our model of policy-embedded learning and information processing, we now turn to avenues for future research. The first avenue concerns the analytical level scalability of this model. As earlier noted, learning occurs within and across various levels, micro, meso, and macro, spanning individuals, collectives (such as advocacy coalitions, policy subsystems, interest groups, and organizations) as well as systemically. Furthermore, learning not only occurs within these levels but also travels across them [@heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013; @dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017;@zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. Because the model specifies clear structural dimensions, including policy actors, information and knowledge, and structures, whether cognitive or institutional, the learning through information processing model is highly scalable across levels. As such, future research can apply this model across multiple levels of analysis, for example, within particular collectives such as networks, advocacy coalitions, or organizations where the underlying mechanisms of interaction between prior beliefs, information processing, and weighted posterior beliefs are assumed at each level. Furthermore, and in terms of analytical level-scalability, this approach could also be applied across levels as, for example, tracing how individual learning connects to coalition learning, which then connects to subsystem learning. The Fukushima vignettes in Chapter 4 offer an initial, illustrative step in this direction. For example, the Germany case traced a single sequence from Chancellor Merkel's individual belief change to a coalition-level preference and behavior shift to a national policy outcome. However, these vignettes were necessarily brief and limited to a small number of cases and extant literature rather than a research design built to test cross-level aggregation systematically, underscoring the need for future work that traces such sequences across a larger and more diverse set of cases.

The second avenue for future research concerns empirically testing the theoretical correspondences identified in Chapter 5 between this model and other perspectives on learning, including its types, modes, and mechanisms. For example, in Chapter 5 we argued that subsystem type predicts learning mode, and that a single formal mechanism can account for both inferential and contingent learning. While these claims were illustrated conceptually, they were not tested empirically. Future work could trace instrumental learning processes empirically by analyzing the processing of information related to secondary beliefs about policy instruments, or test whether subsystem type reliably predicts the mode of learning observed within it, across a larger and more systematic sample of cases than the illustrative Fukushima vignettes.

Finally, research should explore how to connect the learning through information processing model to the study of policy innovation, understood broadly as the adoption, diffusion, and eventual mainstreaming of new policy ideas, instruments, and practices [@goyalNichesMainstreamComputational2025]. Policy innovation and policy learning are closely related in the literature. For example, @kemmerlingSpecialIssuePolicy2023 treats the diffusion of policy innovations from the Global South to the Global North as a form of policy learning. Our model could specify this connection more precisely by treating a jurisdiction's decision to adopt or reject an innovation as a function of the strength of the information signal about that innovation relative to the strength of its own prior beliefs about the policy problem the innovation addresses, which could help explain why some innovations diffuse widely while others remain confined to a small number of early adopters.

This connection would also benefit from attention to which level of government does the learning and the adopting, and to what is being learned. @huangDynamicRoleGovernments2021 shows that in China, higher-level governments play markedly different roles in adopting policy innovations depending on whether they perceive themselves as owning the innovation, acting as proactive facilitators in some cases and gatekeepers in others, a distinction that maps naturally onto the institutional and multi-level structure of the policy-embedded learning framework developed in Chapter 4. Similarly, @wuMarketImperfectionsGovernment2014 traces policy innovation to the instrument mixes jurisdictions adopt in response to the shortcomings of markets and governments alike, which in our terms is a case of instrumental, or secondary-belief, learning. Future work could apply the model developed in this Element to trace how information about an innovation's performance elsewhere is processed, and either adopted, adapted, or rejected, at different levels of government and for different types of beliefs.


## Policy Change Beyond Learning  

While the focus of this Element has been policy learning, there are several other ways in which policy change may occur. It is important to note the limits of our approach as an explanation for policy change overall. For example, ACF scholarship notes that apart from policy-oriented learning policy change, both major (change associated with policy core) and minor (change associated with secondary aspects) can result from events both external and internal to the policy subsystem [@nohrstedtAdvocacyCoalitionFramework2023]. Events or shocks can include changes in socioeconomic conditions, shifts in public opinion, changes in governing arrangements, elections, scandals, policy failures, or crises or disasters. Such events can constitute a strong information signal that leads to policy learning, such as in the cases of the Fukushima accident, the COVID-19 pandemic, or the Russian invasion of Ukraine, among others. However, apart from learning, events can lead to policy change through shifts in the resources available to coalitions or when a coalition pushing for policy change is able to exploit a policy window that opens as a result of the event [@nohrstedtLogicPolicyChange2010]. 

The ACF also notes that policy change can happen as a result of a negotiated agreement between coalitions [@sabatierAdvocacyCoalitionFramework2007]. Negotiated agreements involve deliberation, compromises, and trade-offs between adversarial coalitions, which result in policy changes. Such agreements are more likely in the presence of a "hurting stalemate" or a situation where the status quo is unacceptable to the coalitions, and there are no other policy venues in which to engage [@nohrstedtAdvocacyCoalitionFramework2023]. Finally, policy change can happen as a result of shifts in power between coalitions [@piercePolicyChangeAdvocacy2020]. Power shifts between coalitions can happen as a result of events such as an election that favors elected officials of one coalition, and newly available resources for a coalition such as a powerful elected official, or knowledgeable experts [@nowlinAdvocacyCoalitionsPolitical2022], among others.

While information processing is at the heart of our approach to learning in this element, policy change can also happen as a result of attention to information without any changes in beliefs or preferences [@workmanInformationProcessingPolicy2009]. Policy actors have multiple and perhaps competing policy preferences. Policy change can happen when one preference becomes more salient than another in the absence of learning or preference updating. One example from @jonesReconceivingDecisionMakingDemocratic1994 is the consideration of the US Congress in 1991 and again in 1992 to fund the construction of the superconducting super collider, a particle accelerator that would have been built in that US state of Texas. Seventy-nine US House of Representatives members voted in favor of funding the super collider in 1991 but subsequently voted against funding in 1992. The shift in votes by the seventy-nine members of Congress was likely a result of the issue of the budget deficit gaining more attention and making the preference for a smaller deficit (and perhaps re-election) more salient.

In this Element, we developed a model of policy learning through information processing, applied it to public opinion about nuclear energy following the Fukushima accident, embedded it within a broader policy-embedded learning framework, and returned to the wider policy learning literature to show how this approach speaks to several of the literature's persistent challenges. In our view, this Element has demonstrated the substantial promise of an information-processing approach to enhancing the analytical utility of policy learning research. By tracing how information is processed and reconciled against cognitive and institutional structures, this approach offers a more nuanced understanding of the micro-foundations of policy learning. It also helps advance the analytical utility of different theoretical approaches to learning. By acknowledging the cognitive processes that underpin policy decisions, scholars can gain deeper insights into the dynamics of policy change and the factors that influence learning across different contexts.
